title: Cap. VIII: Chamier ἁμαρτωλούς; Martyr — no sinner by alien vice alone
pass_a_gloss: Placeus prefers Chamier, Garissoles's own forerunner. Chamier insists one must not skip this: many were made sinners — ἁμαρτωλούς — through one person's disobedience, and Scripture uses that word for people who truly have sin against God's law inside them. Shortly after, Chamier adds that ἁμαρτωλὸς never names bare liability alone with no vice or sin present. So Paul's line about many made sinners through one disobedience meant only that Adam's sin brought it about that every human being was a real sinner in himself. Elsewhere Chamier brands as badly false the claim that Paul teaches a single numerically identical original sin in everyone; the verse about many made sinners through one disobedience stands against that claim. Same chapter: a sinner is someone who has his own sin, not someone charged with a stranger's. Again: all sinned in Adam because Adam sinned first and sin thus began in the race; yet we also sin in ourselves, because his sin made us sinners by propagating sin into us. His disobedience made us sinners in the same manner in which we are already truly sinners by our own acts — otherwise the claim that his disobedience made us sinners would be false. Another Chamier locus: we were made sinners through Adam's disobedience causally, not formally; his act efficiently causes the quality by which we are formally sinners — like a gouty father (or gout in the father) causing a gouty son without being the son's gout. Peter Martyr is then heard on the opposing side of the debate: from Paul's words that many were made sinners through one disobedience, one may argue against those who say original sin is not each person's own but only a single sin sitting in Adam that merely binds us to death and damnation. If people are called constituted sinners, they must have sin, or at least have had it. Nobody is named a sinner by a stranger's vice alone. That closes Cap. VIII VI before Caput IX.
pass_b_english: Hear rather his predecessor Chamier. "This too must not be omitted: through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners — ἁμαρτωλούς; which word in the Scriptures is taken for those in whom there truly is sin contrary to God's law." And a little later: "In a word. ἁμαρτωλὸς is never said of bare guilt alone and without any vice or sin. Therefore when Paul said many were constituted sinners through one man's disobedience, he meant nothing else than that by that sin of Adam it was brought about that all human beings were truly sinners in themselves." And elsewhere: that Paul teaches original sin is numerically one in all is strikingly false. For against it stands: "Through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners." In the same chapter: "A sinner is one who himself has his own sin, not one to whom an alien sin is imputed." Again: "In Adam we all sinned, because Adam first sinned, and from that the beginning of sin was made in all human beings; yet we also sin in ourselves, because by his sin we were constituted sinners — that is, sin was propagated from him into us. And by his disobedience we were all constituted sinners in the same way we are already truly sinners by our own; otherwise it would be false that we were constituted sinners by his disobedience." Elsewhere he says we were constituted sinners through Adam's disobedience not formally but causally, because it is the efficient cause of that quality by which we are formally sinners: "Just as," he says, "a gouty parent, or gout in the parent, is the cause of a gouty child, yet is not the child's gout." Hear also Peter Martyr arguing against them. "Here," he says, "we will note that when the Apostle says, 'Through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners,' an argument is had from these words against those who think original sin is not each person's own, but that only one existed, and that it was in Adam, by which we are bound and obligated to death and damnation. For when they are said to be constituted sinners, they themselves must have sin, or at least have had it. For no one is called a sinner by an alien vice."
source_text: Audiamus ergo potius ejus Antecessorem Chamierum, Illud etiam non omittendum: per unius inobedientiam multos esse constitutos peccatores ἁμαρτωλούς; quod vocabulum in Scripturis sumitur pro iis in quibus est re vera peccatum contrarium legi Dei. Et paulo post. Uno verbo. Nunquam ἁμαρτωλὸς dicitur de simplici reatu, & absque ullo vitio aut peccato. Ergo, cum dixit Paulus multos esse constitutos peccatores per unius inobedientiam: NIHIL ALIUD intellexit, nisi eo Adami peccato effectum esse, ut omnes homines re vera, & in se se peccatores essent. Et alio loco, A Paulo autem doceri unicum esse numero in omnibus peccatum originale, hoc vero insigniter falsum. Nam contra. Per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi. Eodem capite. Peccator autem est, qui ipse habet peccatum suum: non autem cui alienum imputatur. Et rursus. In Adamo peccavimus omnes: quia Adamus primus peccavit: & inde initium factum peccati in omnibus hominibus: at in nobis etiam peccamus: quia ejus peccato constituti sumus peccatores: id est, ab eo in nos peccatum propagatum. Et illius inobedientia eodem modo sumus omnes constituti peccatores: quo nostra etiam propria jam vere sumus peccatores: alioqui falsum esset, nos illius inobedientia constitutos esse peccatores. Alio loco ait nos per inobedientiam Adami constitutos esse peccatores, non formaliter, sed causaliter, quia est causa efficiens qualitatis illius per quam sumus formaliter peccatores: Sicut, inquit, podagrici causa est parens podagricus, sive podagra in parente: quae tamen non est podagra filii. Audiamus etiam Petrum Martyrem contra argumentantem. Hic, inquit, annotabimus, cum Apostolus dicit, Per unius inobedientiam peccatores multos esse constitutos, ex his verbis argumentum haberi adversus eos, qui putant peccatum originis non esse cuique proprium: sed unum tantum extitisse, illudque fuisse in Adamo, quo nos nexi, obligati sumus ad mortem & damnationem. Quum enim dicantur peccatores constituti, oportet, ut ipsi aut peccatum habeant, aut saltem habuerint. Nam alieno vitio nemo dicitur peccator.
